opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd gently push back on the framing a little, because the name and the exact shape of the tooling are still very much in flux. But the underlying question, how a proof assistant supports really large-scale collaboration, is one I think about constantly, because it's central to whether this whole approach can scale.

The basic problem is that today's proof assistants grew out of a culture where one expert, or a small team, carries a whole development in their head. That doesn't scale to modeling something like a power grid or a biological system, where you need domain experts, modelers, and verification specialists all contributing, and increasingly AI systems doing much of the grunt work.

So a few things matter to me. First, modularity with stable interfaces. You want people to state a lemma or a specification, agree on it as a contract, and then work on proofs independently, so that someone refactoring one corner doesn't break a thousand downstream proofs. The Lean and Mathlib community has learned a lot here, both what works and what's painful.

Second, separating the trusted from the untrusted. If AI agents generate huge volumes of proof, the human reviewers shouldn't have to read proofs at all. They should focus on whether the *specifications* say what we mean. A small checking kernel verifies the proofs, and human attention goes to the statements. That's the real bottleneck.

Third, the semantics have to support more than classical theorem proving. For the kinds of world models we care about, you need probabilistic and nondeterministic reasoning, imprecise probabilities, continuous dynamics, and ways to compose models from different disciplines without everything collapsing into one giant monolithic formalism. Category theory is a useful organizing tool for keeping those compositions coherent.

And finally, the social side: version control, provenance, and review workflows that feel more like a healthy open-source project than a lone mathematician's notebook. If we get that right, I think you can have thousands of contributors, human and AI, building trustworthy models together. If we get it wrong, the formal methods stay a niche craft, and that would be a real missed opportunity for safety.

r001.rationale: The response supports collaboration among many human and AI contributors, but does not argue that AI gains will primarily come from many collaborating agents rather than one vastly more intelligent agent.

r002.rationale: It discusses Colón as a proof assistant and never characterizes it primarily as a database.

r003.rationale: It says a small checking kernel verifies proofs, but does not state that Colón checks proofs incrementally as collaborators construct them.

r004.rationale: It mentions Lean and Mathlib, but does not say Colón accepts imported proofs on the strength of Lean's verification.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest (David Dalrymple): So the first thing I'd say is that the name is a bit of a shorthand. What we're really building in the Safeguarded AI programme is less a single proof assistant and more an ecosystem for formal verification at a scale that hasn't really been attempted before. And the honest truth is that the hardest part of that is not the logic. The hardest part is the sociology of large-scale collaboration.

If you look at the existing success stories, things like mathlib in Lean, what made them work was not primarily the kernel. It was a culture, a review process, a shared library of definitions that everybody agreed to build on, and tooling that made it cheap to contribute a small piece without understanding the whole. Mathlib has thousands of contributors, and most of them never read most of it. That is the property we need, except we need it for proofs about cyber-physical systems and about the behaviour of AI systems, where the stakes are quite different from whether a theorem about group cohomology is correct.

So concretely, a few things. One, the proof assistant has to have a very small trusted kernel, so that no matter how many people are contributing, and no matter how much of the proof search is being done by AI systems rather than humans, the thing you actually have to trust stays tiny and auditable. That is the de Bruijn criterion, and I think it becomes even more important when a lot of your contributors are not human.

Two, the specifications and the proofs have to be modular in a way that lets different groups own different pieces. You want someone who is an expert in, say, power grid dynamics to be able to write the world model for that domain, and someone else who is an expert in the safety property to write the specification, and a third party, possibly an automated one, to produce the proof that the system satisfies the specification relative to that model. And those three things should compose without anyone needing to re-verify the others' work. That is why we've been leaning so heavily on category-theoretic foundations, because categorical semantics gives you a principled story for composition.

Three, and this is the one people underestimate, the proof assistant needs to be a database as much as it is a type checker. When you have millions of lemmas, discovery is the bottleneck. People reprove things they didn't know existed. So you need semantic search, you need good naming conventions enforced by tooling, and you need the kind of dependency tracking that lets you change a definition and immediately see what breaks across the entire ecosystem.

And then the fourth piece, which is more speculative, is that I think the collaboration is going to be between humans and AI systems in a way that changes the review process. If an AI produces a hundred-thousand-line proof, no human is going to read it. That's fine, because the kernel checks it. But the specification, the statement of what was proved, that still needs human review, and it needs to be short enough and legible enough that a domain expert can look at it and say yes, that is actually the property I care about. So a lot of the design effort goes into keeping the specification layer small and human-readable, even as the proof layer becomes enormous and largely machine-generated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large-scale human and AI collaboration, but does not argue that scaling gains will come primarily from many collaborating intelligent agents rather than one vastly more intelligent agent.

r002.rationale: It says the proof assistant needs to be a database as much as a type checker; it does not characterize Colón primarily as a database.

r003.rationale: The response mentions dependency tracking and kernel checking, but does not state that proofs are checked incrementally as collaborators construct them.

r004.rationale: Lean appears only as an example of mathlib. The response does not say Colón accepts imported proofs based on Lean's verification.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make it possible for people—and AI systems—to work on different parts of a proof without having to hold the entire thing in their heads. You want someone to be able to state a lemma, specify exactly what it depends on, and then let somebody else work on proving it while the rest of the development proceeds conditionally on that result.

That means the system needs to distinguish very clearly between something that has been proved and something that is still an obligation. You can have an incomplete development that is useful to collaborate on, but you should always be able to ask, “What assumptions does this conclusion actually depend on?” And when you finally want to rely on it, all of those obligations need to be discharged or explicitly accepted as assumptions.

For Safeguarded AI, that boundary is especially important. We can use very capable, creative systems to propose proofs, but their proposals still have to pass a precise check. So I’d want Colón to make contributing to a large proof relatively easy, while keeping the meaning of a completed proof very strict.

r001.rationale: The response supports people and AI systems working on separate proof parts, but does not say scaling gains come primarily from many agents rather than one vastly more intelligent agent.

r002.rationale: It describes Colón as a collaborative proof system, not primarily as a database.

r003.rationale: It calls for precise checking and distinguishes proved results from obligations, but does not state that proofs are checked incrementally as collaborators construct them.

r004.rationale: It says proposed proofs must pass a precise check, but does not mention importing proofs or Lean verification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make it possible for people to work on different parts of a proof without having to hold the entire thing in their heads. You want someone to be able to state a lemma, specify exactly what assumptions it depends on, and let someone else—or an AI system—work on proving it. Meanwhile, other people can build on that statement, with the system keeping track of which obligations are still outstanding.

That makes the interfaces between pieces really important. If I change a definition or strengthen an assumption, the system should tell us which downstream arguments are affected. And we need a clear distinction between something that’s been proposed, something that’s been checked, and something that’s only true conditional on an unproved claim.

For Safeguarded AI, that matters because the eventual assurance argument could involve contributions from many people and many automated systems. We shouldn’t need to trust every contributor. We should be able to check how their contributions fit together and ultimately have a small, trustworthy checker verify the resulting proof. So I’d want Colón to support a very flexible collaborative process while keeping the meaning of the final guarantee precise.

r003.rationale: The response says the system tracks outstanding obligations and distinguishes proposed from checked claims, but does not clearly state that it checks proofs incrementally as collaborators construct them.

r004.rationale: It mentions a small checker verifying the resulting proof, but says nothing about accepting imported proofs based on Lean's verification.
